title: Priscilla is one of those names you can read in seconds…
paragraphs:
Priscilla is one of those names you can read in seconds…
and miss for a lifetime.

She doesn’t have a book named after her.
She didn’t stand before kings like Paul.
She didn’t preach to thousands like Peter.
But heaven recorded her impact anyway.
And if you look closely, her story carries a weight most people overlook.

Acts 18 introduces us to a man named Apollos.
He was eloquent. Passionate. Gifted.
The kind of speaker people would stop and listen to.

Scripture says he was “mighty in the Scriptures.”
That means he knew the Word. He could teach it. He had fire.
But then comes a quiet detail that changes everything:
“He knew only the baptism of John.”
In other words—he was powerful… but incomplete.
And this is where Priscilla steps into the story.

Not on a stage.
Not in front of a crowd.
Not to correct him publicly.
But privately.
“Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.” (Acts 18:26)
Don’t rush past that.
They took him aside.

No embarrassment.
No platform correction.
No public humiliation.
Just wisdom… in a quiet room.
That alone is a lesson many people miss.

Because immature people love to expose others.
Mature people know how to restore them.

Priscilla saw something rare:
A man full of potential… with a gap in understanding.

And instead of criticizing his gap,
she invested in his growth.
That takes discernment.
That takes humility.
That takes security in your calling.

Because not everyone can sit across from someone gifted
and not feel threatened.

Not everyone can see brilliance
and still choose to build it instead of compete with it.
But Priscilla could.
And here’s what makes this even more powerful:
After this moment… Apollos becomes even more effective.
Scripture says he “powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.” (Acts 18:28)
Do you see it?

The man who was already strong
became sharper.

The preacher who was already gifted
became clearer.

And behind that transformation…
was a woman most people barely notice.
Priscilla.

This is the kind of impact that doesn’t trend.
It doesn’t go viral.
It doesn’t get applause.
But it moves heaven.

Because the kingdom of God has always advanced
through people who were willing to build others quietly.
And here’s the truth most people don’t want to hear:

Not every calling is meant to be visible.
But every calling is meant to be faithful.

Some people are called to preach.
Some are called to plant.
Some are called to correct, guide, and sharpen those who will.
And none of those roles are lesser.

We just live in a world that celebrates microphones
more than maturity.
But Scripture doesn’t.
In fact, something very interesting happens in the New Testament:
Multiple times, Priscilla’s name is mentioned before Aquila’s (Romans 16:3, 2 Timothy 4:19).
That was culturally unusual.

Which suggests something powerful—
her influence was not small.

She was not silent in impact.
She was significant in function.

She helped lead a house church.
She helped disciple believers.
And in this moment, she helped refine a preacher who would impact many.
That is not background work.
That is kingdom work.
And maybe this is where it becomes personal.
Because some of you feel overlooked right now.

You’re not the one being celebrated.
You’re not the one being seen.
You’re not the one on the platform.

But you are pouring into someone.
Encouraging someone.
Correcting someone with love.
Helping someone understand truth more clearly.
And it feels small.
But it’s not.
Because you don’t always see the full reach of who you’re helping.

Priscilla probably didn’t know
how far Apollos’ voice would travel.
But God did.

And that’s what makes faithfulness so powerful—
you don’t need full visibility to have eternal impact.
Let this settle in your spirit:

You don’t have to be the loudest voice
to be a powerful one.

You don’t have to be seen by crowds
to be known by heaven.

And you don’t have to hold the stage
to shape the message that reaches it.
Priscilla reminds us of a deeper kind of influence.

The kind that doesn’t shout…
but transforms.

The kind that doesn’t perform…
but prepares.

The kind that doesn’t compete…
but completes.
So don’t despise your role.

Don’t shrink your assignment
just because it doesn’t look like someone else’s.

And don’t overlook the quiet work
God has placed in your hands.

Because one conversation…
one correction…
one moment of obedience…

can shape a voice
that echoes farther than you ever will.
And that is not small.
That is sacred.
So here’s the question:

Are you willing to be a Priscilla—
faithful in the quiet,
focused on building others,
and secure enough to shape what you may never stand in?

Or are you still waiting for a stage
God never asked you to stand on?
